subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
subsubtopic: CALL FOR AMENDMENTS TO GUN CONTROL REGULATIONS- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, in connection with the gun control legislation.
Everywhere across this nation, law-abiding citizens are appalled by the administration of this act, which has become a bureaucratic jumble of misinterpretations which differ among enforcement officers, with the consequent result that injustices occurring to good and responsible citizens, and in particular to sportsmen and sportswomen, are creating grave concern except to the underworld, which is making fabulous profits in illicit sales of firearms.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski):
That before this House adjourns, a committee be set up with power to bring about needed amendments to the regulations, to the end that uniformity of interpretation be achieved and injustices to responsible individuals be done away with.

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
subsubtopic: DEVALUED CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON UNEMPLOYMENT-EMPLOYMENT TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. It relates to the recently released figures with respect to unemployment which show there are still one million people unemployed in this country, including the hidden jobless.
This is nothing to be pleased about; we should be ashamed of those figures. What is even more significant is the fact that in the industrial heartland of Ontario, the city of Windsor is suffering from unemployment at a rate of 10.2 per cent, in Sudbury the rate is 12 per cent, in Hamilton 8 per cent, in St. Catharines 14.5 per cent, and in parts of the Niagara region, it reaches 20 per cent.
Does the minister consider this matter to be serious, and how does he intend to reverse this very unacceptable situation, particularly when he brags about how well manufacturing is doing and what the devalued dollar is doing in terms of job creation?

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
subsubtopic: DEVALUED CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON UNEMPLOYMENT-EMPLOYMENT TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to report to the House that in the manufacturing sector, in the last 12 months, 159,000 new jobs were created, an increase of 8.7 per cent from the previous year, that unemployment went down by two-tenths of a point in Ontario, and that the Canadian economy managed to put 400,000 more people to work last month than in the same month last year.
I think that is good news. It is a good trend. It is not the end of the problem we face, but one has to recognize that we are making progress. Of course, when hon. members opposite have only doom and gloom in mind, it is hard for them to see any ray of sunshine on the horizon.
Oral Questions

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
subsubtopic: DEVALUED CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON UNEMPLOYMENT-EMPLOYMENT TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister should stop misleading the Canadian people. One million people out of work is nothing to sneer and gloat about. We are calling for action.
I will give the minister an opportunity to do something which perhaps can get him out of the mess he is in. The employment tax credit was supposed to create some 50,000 jobs. We are short by about 34,000 jobs. Will the minister, together with the minister he is talking to now, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion get together with their provincial counterparts to determine what to do about the cities I just spoke about-I mentioned Windsor, Sudbury, Hamilton, St. Catharines and the Niagara region-in order to create the 34,000 jobs which have not been created yet? Will the minister do that, instead of gloating about how happy he is that one million people are unemployed?

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
subsubtopic: DEVALUED CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON UNEMPLOYMENT-EMPLOYMENT TAX CREDIT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since it has been implemented, the employment tax credit program has created 16,700 jobs. I am informed that the business community realizes the advantages of this tax credit for the creation of new jobs. There is a take-up under this program of 500 jobs a week. We had to make some changes in the regulations after we started the program, and the program is starting to pick up some steam. It is helping to create jobs in the private sector; but the hon. member does not want to see the evidence.

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
subsubtopic: DEVALUED CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON UNEMPLOYMENT-EMPLOYMENT TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I said yesterday that the minister was full of boloney, and I say that he is full of boloney again today. What he has conveniently forgotten to tell the Canadian people is that 9,000 of those 16,000 jobs were created in the province of Quebec. That means that there is a tremendous shortfall in the rest of the country.
The minister evaded my question. Will he meet with his counterparts in the province of Ontario, together with the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, to see how the slack in the employment tax credit can be picked up? Will the minister answer that question, instead of giving me a lot of flim-flam?

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not impressed by the loud voice of the hon. member. I think the take-up under this new program is pretty good. The hon. member can see that in some parts of the country the program has been used to better advantage than in other parts. Because there was some slowdown in the province of Ontario, I hope more advantage will be taken. If new personnel are put on the payrolls, the advantage will be $1.50 per hour in terms of tax credits. I think this is a good program. It is available to everyone. I hope the businessmen who listen to this argument will realize that there is unanimity in this House that it is a good program.

UNEMPLOYMENT IN EASTERN CANADA-CALL FOR SPECIAL PROGRAM TO ALLEVIATE SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers. The unemployment figures

released today show, no matter what consolation the government can take from them nationally, that Atlantic Canada, and in particular Newfoundland, is still suffering high unemployment even after all the government's wishful thinking that things are getting better.
The real unemployment rate in Newfoundland is still over 30 per cent, with New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island at over 25 per cent and Nova Scotia at around 18 per cent. Is this sufficient evidence to convince the minister that a special economic program is needed to alleviate the real economic difficulties suffered by individual Canadians in eastern Canada, a program that should of necessity involve tax cuts to lower and middle income people, and investment in housing and public works? Will the minister now consider this sort of program?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT IN EASTERN CANADA-CALL FOR SPECIAL PROGRAM TO ALLEVIATE SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 do not think that kind of program would alleviate the problems to which the hon. member referred. Without in any way indicating our lack of concern for it, because we are very concerned about it, the hon. member knows that a great deal of the problem in the area to which he referred is a seasonal one.
There are many programs of the federal government at work now. The retiring premier of that province has indicated that Newfoundland is poised for prosperity. I doubt very much that panic measures such as the hon. member is suggesting would, in fact, alleviate the unemployment and l think they would cause severe problems in other directions.

subtopic: HIGH UNEMPLOYMENT AND INFLATION IN EASTERN CANADA- EFFECT ON CONSUMERS
HIGH UNEMPLOYMENT AND INFLATION IN EASTERN CANADA- EFFECT ON CONSUMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the retiring premier might say the province is poised for prosperity, but to unemployed people along the coast who make up 30 per cent of the workforce of the province there is certainly no prosperity there.
I should like to address my supplementary question to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. The unemployment rates that I have mentioned present a picture of real hardship for people in Newfoundland and the other Atlantic provinces when viewed with the inflation figures for the area. Inflation in Newfoundland is running at the highest rate in Canada, with last month's increase at an annual rate of some 9 per cent.
Has the minister made any investigation as to why inflation rates in the Newfoundland region of slow growth are the highest in Canada, in a region that can least afford high inflation and, if not, will he undertake to see why consumers in Newfoundland are being hit with a double whammy, the highest unemployment in Canada along with the highest prices?

THE SEAL HUNT
subsubtopic: ALLEGED INHUMANE TREATMENT WHICH WILL ENDANGER SPECIES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment. Given all the fuss which is being made about the seal hunt and in order to calm people down and reassure the public, would the minister be in a position to tell the House whether illegal hunting is actually taking place, whether the methods used are cruel and whether the number of seal pups which will be killed is high enough to endanger the very existence of the herd in the region in question?

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
subtopic: THE SEAL HUNT
subsubtopic: ALLEGED INHUMANE TREATMENT WHICH WILL ENDANGER SPECIES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member will recall there was a lot of controversy in Canada a few years ago. The more
Oral Questions
we inform the public, the more they agree that this hunt is absolutely legal, that it is comparable with other activities consisting in killing animals for the meat they provide. It is somewhat brutal, that cannot be denied. This having been said, however, the hunt is carried out under the strict control of persons fully cognizant with fisheries. It is carried out in the presence of people working for groups whose aim is to prevent animal cruelty. I must say that if all animals were killed in a way as tightly controlled and as disciplined as the seals are, there would be no protests whatsoever.

subtopic: THE SEAL HUNT
subsubtopic: ALLEGED INHUMANE TREATMENT WHICH WILL ENDANGER SPECIES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the minister. I want to thank him for his very precise answer. I should like therefore to ask him to tell the House whether these sectors of our industry are yielding rather substantial income for Canada, and whether his departmental officials are taking the necessary steps to preserve this species, so that we may continue to use it in a humane fashion, as he has just indicated.

subtopic: THE SEAL HUNT
subsubtopic: ALLEGED INHUMANE TREATMENT WHICH WILL ENDANGER SPECIES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can assure the hon. member that no evidence has been produced to indicate that it is in any danger, as far as conservation is concerned. On the contrary, we have set very low quotas to favour a quicker restoration of our stocks. As to the economic aspect, I must say that compared with other sectors of activities, these few millions of dollars may appear modest. But when we consider that this represents one third of their yearly income for a great many fishermen, either from the Magdalen Islands or Newfoundland, I think that we should be ill advised to accept the views of foreigners who are taking advantage of this protest to make money.

of information. I think he should either drop me a line or put a question on the order paper and I will get the specifics back to him.

speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I understand that the minister is not overly concerned with what has happened to the beneficiairies rendered ineligible by Bill C-14. Since the unemployment rate has dropped from 8.1 to 7.9 per cent, and I think the minister is aware that a number of people, discouraged by the provisions of this bill and the fact that jobs are hard to find did not file new job applications with manpower centres, which may explain the apparent drop in the unemployment rate since the Statistics Canada figures hide the true unemployment rate, will the minister undertake to request a study to determine what has happened to these people? Mr. Speaker, I do not know that the supply of additional information is going to be beneficial. The fact of the matter is that the participation rate in Canada this year among the working force is higher, rather than lower.
We have also indicated to various provinces, particularly to the welfare officers, that if they find people are constantly unemployed, will not be drawing unemployment insurance benefits and this would impact on their welfare rolls or welfare payments, we will make a special study of this situation and make additional efforts to see what we can do either to train them or to put them back in the work force. But to suggest that the numbers are down is not correct; the participation rate is higher this year than last year.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ISSUANCE OF LAPEL PINS TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I would like to borrow for just a moment from the time of the House to reflect on an activity that was undertaken and given considerable study by our Standing

March 13, 1979
Lapel Pins
Committee on Management and Members Services. It relates to the bringing into existence of a lapel pin to be given to an elected member of the House of Commons. I have the first of such pins here with me.
For some time we have been aware that other parliaments have had an identifying emblem of some sort given to those who have had the honour to serve their fellow citizens in an elected capacity in the national legislature of their country. We have not done so.
Some time ago this committee, under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates) and the vice-chairmanship of the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Duquet), commissioned a subcommittee to study the matter. The work of that subcommittee resulted in a recommendation which in fact was carried forward in consultation with me to bring this lapel pin into existence. I should mention that the subcommittee was headed by a very distinguished and senior member of the House, a former Speaker of the House of Commons, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert).

subtopic: ISSUANCE OF LAPEL PINS TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ISSUANCE OF LAPEL PINS TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
This is a milestone in Canadian parliamentary history, that recognition is being given to those who serve in this House of Commons. They ought at least to have some emblem they can carry, one that they have been able to earn and which is received only by election to this House of Commons of Canada as a recognition of all that that entails and the serious responsibility that goes with it. I want to congratulate and thank the members of the committee for their excellent work.
I might say that this identifying pin for elected members of this House is in conjunction with a program that is still under study and being perfected in some detail. It will likely be put before the House for approval in the next parliament. That program relates to a further identification of other personnel in the House in the security context. I do not want to cast this pin in the security context, although it has an incidental relationship to security. This is an emblem of election to the House of Commons.
It gives me great pleasure to ask four members, representing each of the four parties of the House, to come forward now and receive one of these pins: the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier).

subsubtopic: MR. YEWCHUK-RESPONSE OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) raised as a question of privilege some remarks that had been made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) during the course of the question period. The contention of the hon. member for Athabasca was that, in answering his first question yesterday in the question period, the minister had said that the hon. member was acting in the capacity of a lobbyist. I indicated after argument that I would review the remarks of the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
I did review those remarks after I listened to argument on the question. Here is the full quote by the minister at the time as it appears in yesterday's Hansard'.
Mr. Speaker, since the hon. member is of the profession, he may be naturally asked by his friends to be a lobbyist in the House in favour of higher fees for medical doctors.
The fact that the hon. member may be asked by his friends to carry out a certain function surely is not in any way unparliamentary, nor does not in any way carry with it an allegation of an unparliamentary activity. 1 do not decide now and I do not think I have to decide. Had the minister gone on to accuse the member or any other member of being a lobbyist in fact, which is a sort of paid or hired position, I do not know whether that would be unparliamentary in nature. In fact, 1 am relieved of that responsibility because the language used by the minister, and it was my recollection that was so, had indicated that the hon. member may be asked by his friends to carry out that function. It did not go on to say that the member was in fact doing so. In the circumstances, I would find that falls short of anything unparliamentary.

subtopic: ENERGY SUPPLIES EMERGENCY ACT, 1979 MEASURES TO CONSERVE STOCKS

speechtext:
The House resumed from Monday, March 12, consideration of Bill C-42, to provide a means to conserve the supplies of

energy within Canada during periods of national emergency caused by shortages or market disturbances affecting the national security and welfare and the economic stability of Canada, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works, and Motion No. 1 (Mr. Gillespie).

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ENERGY SUPPLIES EMERGENCY ACT, 1979 MEASURES TO CONSERVE STOCKS
speechtext:
Yesterday, a point of order was raised with regard to the procedural regulatory of motion No. 1 at the report stage of Bill C-42. That point of order was supported by several arguments. It was contended that the motion was out of order because it introduced into the bill a new concept by giving the board created by Bill C-42 a role in monitoring the international petroleum supply situation. The argument was that this was a new role for the board, that it caused the board to do things entirely separate from its original capacity under Bill C-42, and, therefore, that it was out of order on that ground.
It was also argued that if the first amendment was in order because the function of monitoring petroleum supplies is incidental to the function of the board in regulating an emergency situation for petroleum, the additional concept of responsibility to be given by the minister in that regard to Petro-Canada was a new concept and ought not to be part of an amendment to a bill at this stage.
I considered most of those arguments yesterday. There was an argument that because these amendments had not been put forward in previous stages of the bill, they could not be put forward at the report stage, and I set that aside yesterday.
I also found yesterday that the function of monitoring international petroleum supplies seemed, at least to me, to be sufficiently incidental to the role of the board in these circumstances and that on procedural grounds 1 could not consider that the amendment related to the function.
Whether those arguments form a part of the substance of the debate once it begins is not for me to decide. I have to decide whether the amendment is out of order, and if the amendment were out of order on that basis, I think the function would have to be so unrelated as to be clearly a new concept introduced into the bill at this stage. It is a separate role from that which is set up in Bill C-42, but I cannot find that it is an unrelated function. Therefore, I cannot find that the amendment is out of order on that ground.
This leaves me with the matter of the procedural capacity of an amendment to introduce into this bill a role for Petro-Canada, and I said I would give serious consideration to that argument, which was put forward by the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre). I have done so.
What gave me concern on the face of it-and the hon. member for Calgary Centre as well and others who participated in the discussion-was, of course, the precedents which relate to procedural difficulties where an amendment to this bill would in effect reach behind this bill and attempt to amend another statute. I have, first of all, some guidance from
March 13, 1979

the precedents as to what extent I should concern myself with that problem, because there is a considerable body of argument which states that the Chair ought not to concern itself with what may in effect require an amendment of another statute or may incidentally amend another statute or may even in fact be in conflict with the provisions of another statute. That is not the decision of the Chair because that requires a legal interpretation.
Here I want to refer the House to a precedent in Hansard of May 6 of 1969 by my predecessor at that time who said the following:
I think there is a substantial difference between a proposed amendment that obviously seeks directly to amend the original legislation and one that, by way of consequence, might require amendments which, as is in this case, are not of a substantive nature.
In other words, that is an expression of the proposition that the Chair obviously must be on guard to the situation where the reference to the other statute of Petro-Canada would be clearly in terms of an attempt to amend that statute by adding a clause or things of that nature, or in fact by amending the statute itself in explicit language to attempt to do so.
That is one thing. It is rather a second question for the Chair to take one step further and to listen to the argument that, if this clause is put before the House and passed, it will have the incidental effect of amending another statute or requiring an amendment to another statute to be effective. That may be so, but that is essentially a legal question which is really not an area the Chair should get into in matters of this sort. For that proposition again I refer to a 1969 precedent by Mr. Speaker Lamoureux reported at page 7969 of Hansard.
My feeling, however, is that the Chair should not be placed in a position where the Speaker has to rule on legal points. The tradition and background of the position of the Chair is that the Speaker should rule only on procedural matters.
It therefore ought not to be for the Chair now to look at the Petro-Canada statute and decide whether the statute gives to Petro-Canada the power that the minister seeks to give it in this statute by way of this amendment. However, I am at least somewhat affected by the language in section 3 of that statute which is entitled "Purpose of the Act" and reads in part as follows:
The purpose of this Act is to establish within the energy industries in Canada a Crown owned company with authority to explore for hydro-carbon deposits-
And here is the significant language:
-to negotiate for and acquire petroleum and petroleum products from abroad to assure a continuity of supply for the needs of Canada-
Therefore, I think on balance I have to conclude that, with the role which is assigned to me to look at this matter on procedural grounds, I would have to be examining a situation where there was in clear language an attempt to add a clause to that statute or, by its very own language, to amend that statute, whereas here there is simply a use of the corporation created by that statute. I think it is not for the Chair to go beyond the procedural responsibility I have and try to make a legal interpretation as to whether that can or should be done, or whether it is going to be in conflict with other legislative provisions. I have to decide whether it so introduces a new
Energy Supplies
concept into this statute that it goes beyond the regulations, precedents and practices that we have governing amendments to legislation.
On the whole I have to find, after listening to arguments on both sides, that I am left in some uncertainty and doubt about whether that point has been established, and I think in these circumstances I ought to resolve the doubt in favour of keeping the matter before the House so that the House will debate it, discuss it and vote upon it. In other words, I ought only to take away from the House the right to discuss measures if I am absolutely convinced that they are out of order. In this case I am left in some doubt, and therefore I think I have to resolve that doubt by having the House deal with the matter.
Therefore, on procedural grounds I see no basis upon which I ought to interrupt the putting of the motion. I believe the motion has been formally put. Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the said motion?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: ENERGY SUPPLIES EMERGENCY ACT, 1979 MEASURES TO CONSERVE STOCKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like just briefly to go over some of the background to this amendment and to put before the House some of the events which I think make this amendment important, extremely relevant and urgent at this time.
Hon. members will recall, as we got into the second reading debate, some of the events which led the government to bring this particular bill before the House. I refer, of course, to the revolution in Iran, the cessation of oil production in Iran, the reduction of world supplies by close to six million barrels a day and the absolute economic and energy paralysis of the world's second largest oil producer and exporter.
Those events in Iran created a ripple effect around the world. It was not very long before those events in Iran were felt on the east coast of Canada. Hon. members are familiar with the fact that there were cutbacks, that a number of Canadian refiners had been dependent upon Iranian supplies, that Iranian supplies amounted to close to 100,000 barrels a day, roughly 20 per cent of Canadian import needs, and that a large part of eastern Canada, sometimes described as one third of Canada-the Atlantic provinces and a substantial part of the Quebec market-was completely dependent upon foreign supplies. Cutbacks began to occur. Reallocations started to be made between the supply companies which were providing oil to eastern refineries.
Hon. members will also be familiar with the fact that the Exxon Corporation, in allocating to its subsidiary in Canada, Imperial Oil, went overboard. It was proposing a diversion of supplies equivalent to about 25 per cent of the imports of Imperial Oil into Canada. It should also be noted that Imperial Oil's almost exclusive source-not completely but almost exclusive source-has been Venezuela. Let it also be noted that Venezuela has been our most reliable and largest supplier of imported crude oil for the longest time, some 40 to 50 years, without any interruption of supply. Let it also be noted that in early January the Venezuelan government gave a commitment to me that it wished to continue to do business with Canada

March 13, 1979
Energy Supplies
and to supply Canada, its second most important customer, with 200,000 barrels a day. They also wished, so far as possible, to deal directly with importers in Canada rather than through third parties or the Exxon Corporation.
For those two reasons-the reason that Venezuela had given in the sense of assurances for a continuing supply to Canada, and the fact that Imperial Oil was virtually exclusively sourcing from Venezuela-we had reason to believe that Canada and that particular company would have been helped on this in the event of the kinds of reallocations that were taking place as the result of the events in Iran. The effect was not a cutback on any pro rata basis within the Exxon Corporation. What Exxon had proposed to Imperial was an entirely different formula. They had intervened with their own arrangements which clearly undercut the security of supply for Canada.
As a matter of policy, the Canadian government has been trying to increase the security of supply for Canada by sourcing in the western hemisphere. That was the reason for my trip to Venezuela and my trip to Mexico as well. The Mexicans equally were forthcoming. They too said they wanted to deal with Canada, and they too said they wanted to give preference to Canada, a western hemisphere neighbour. They too said they wanted to deal directly, and they gave us an undertaking to supply Canada with 100,000 barrels a day of crude starting in late 1980 or early 1981.
Those two undertakings-the Venezuelan undertaking and the Mexican undertaking-can shift our dependence away from the Middle East in a signficant way. They can increase the security of supply for Canada in a dramatic way from something like 40 per cent in the western hemisphere to 60 per cent in the western hemisphere; or, to put it another way, they can reduce our dependence on Middle Eastern and eastern hemisphere sources from 60 per cent to 40 per cent, and do that within a relatively short space of time.
Since this bill was introduced, a number of other events have occurred which have added a sense of urgency to the situation at present. I am talking about the fact that while the Iranian government has stated it will be resuming oil production, it has not indicated it will get up to anything like full production. The Iranians have stated they may be able to get up to one half of their original production levels, and that is obviously something which we can greet with some enthusiasm and encouragement, but it still leaves a significant shortfall of some three million barrels a day. In other words, there will be smaller volumes from Iran for some time.
There are also going to be, as a result of the policy in Iran, higher prices. The new regime there has indicated they will charge everything the traffic will bear. They have indicated they will auction to the highest price. They have stated they will look for $5 and even $10 per barrel premiums, and their statement and this shortage are creating an uneasiness in some of the other suppliers, because they too are faced with political pressures at home and they too are having to answer to their constituents why they should sell for less if Iran can get more.

So we have seen a series of events in the Persian Gulf. Countries have been raising prices and announcing increases in prices. We have seen as well the action of the Libyan government which has not only raised prices but has stated it will cut production. These are recent events, not altogether unpredictable but events that have occurred since the introduction of this bill.
At the same time, we have witnessed the increasing isolation of Saudi Arabia. The events in Iran have created an entirely different situation in the Middle East. We have seen the kind of expeditions that have been launched in South Yemen and North Yemen that have been described as border disputes, but these two states are on the southern border of Saudi Arabia. One of the states is described as a Soviet satellite run by a Marxist government in an increasingly Marxist area of the world. I am referring, of course, to the borders of Afghanistan and to the element which has been developing within Iran itself. And there are all of the additional tensions that have been created there.
We have also seen, to our regret and disappointment, the inability of Mr. Carter, President of the United States, to bring a degree of stability and understanding between two of the main combatants, two of the main states of the Middle East, Israel and Egypt, to the bargaining table. The events in Iran have not helped because the government of Iran has stated it would no longer continue the policy of the shah to supply oil to Israel.
I think I have said enough to indicate that the events in the Middle East are less stable today than they were even a few weeks ago when this bill was first addressed at second reading. I should like to say that perhaps in two weeks' time the situation will be better, but 1 would be a foolish man if I were to predict that degree of improvement.
The other question that has arisen since this bill was introduced is how a shortfall might be allocated. The International Energy Agency of which Canada is a member by treaty has agreed to joint action which would reduce world demand by two million barrels a day, roughly 5 per cent of the consumption of the IEA countries. That 5 per cent figure is very close to the 7 per cent figure which is the figure which will trigger our treaty obligations and the need for this bill, the mandatory allocation of crude oil, the mandatory allocation of products and possibly the introduction of a rationing scheme.
I emphasized two things in these remarks, the fact that the IEA is closer than it has ever been since its inception to dealing with the very reason that it was created, and the fact that the process of allocating international crude and crude movements will be undertaken and influenced to a large extent by multinational corporations, by the internationals themselves.
In the debate yesterday on whether or not this motion was in order there was some discussion about this. The energy critic of the Conservative party put it on the record that the International Energy Agency was set up with a standing group on emergency questions and he indicated that the standing group will be composed of one or more representatives of the govern-
March 13, 1979

ment of each participating country. I am referring to article 54 of the institutional and general provisions of the International Energy Agency.
The amendment which has been introduced would name Petro-Canada to the standing group on emergency questions. It is the senior operative executive committee concerned with the implementation of the emergency oil-sharing arrangement. We believe that Petro-Canada's nomination as one of the Canadian government representatives is appropriate entirely, and more than that, it is essential in light of the manner in which the international allocation process will be undertaken.
It is quite clear from the institutional structure of the organization that international companies will play a major role, both in an advisory manner and in an implementing manner. Therefore, it is all the more important for Canada that Petro-Canada represent the interests of Canadians in the highest executive committee, the standing group on emergency questions, not just to advise Canada and other Canadian representatives who might be present, but to maintain a watchdog influence respecting the implementation process to ensure Canada is dealt with in a fair manner.
I would not want to suggest that other countries will not live up to their treaty obligations in the event we are faced collectively with our obligation under the international energy agency oil-sharing agreement of 7 per cent. But there is the possibility some countries will try to take advantage of the situation and will try to over-protect their own interests in a manner which could be harmful to Canada. Also it is quite possible that those countries might be served by their own international companies. It does not take any great imagination to see that an international oil corporation, which will be involved in this very difficult implementation process, could favour some countries to the disadvantage of others. Also it is well known that Canada does not have any international company which might be able to look out for Canada's interests. It is for that reason I believe the addition of Petro-Canada to the standing group on emergency questions is important.
I believe the events with Imperial and Exxon have demonstrated that we will have to depend increasingly upon ourselves to solve our own problems.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I must say most of us in the House, at least on this side, were rather disappointed at the rather lacklustre and fragmentary exposition of the problems we in Canada face today as a result of the lack of a meaningful national policy on energy, oil and gas in the country over the last ten years.

speechtext:
The clear import of what the minister said, in regard to any potential crisis we may have in the country respecting energy supply, is that he has absolutely no policy whatsoever except to lean heavily on a state-owned but not necessarily state-controlled oil company to bail him out of his oil supply problems. When the minister indicated that Exxon, the parent company of Imperial Oil, went overboard in regard to its attempted cutbacks respecting its Canadian subsidiary, Imperial Oil, I must say I agree with him. I do not think there is any question about that.
In the complex marketing, purchasing, wholesaling and distribution set-up of the oil and gas industry in the country, I fail to see how the imposition of one large state-run oil company in that complicated chain of events will be any improvement whatsoever over the efforts, and sometimes unsuccessful efforts in our interest, of a large multinatinal oil company. To my mind, all the minister is doing is substituting big government for a big company. There are many, many other reasonable, sensible and meaningful alternatives than that. If that is the best the minister can come up with, I am sure all he is doing is assisting the control and supervision of many of these matters by a state-run oil company. speechtext:
If there are not, whose fault is it if it is not the fault of the government? What has this particular government done over the last ten years to develop and promote smaller Canadian companies in the resource field? Absolutely nothing. The tax situation, the development situation and the promotion situation over the last ten years have been simply that. Certainly there have been bona fide efforts by some

March 13, 1979

provincial governments in the resource field to do exactly that. As a matter of fact, in the exploration and drilling sectors of the industry at the moment there is a growing control of exploration for oil and gas in the country by smaller Canadian-owned, controlled and managed companies. There are many, but they are not there because of the atmosphere generated by the government; they are there in spite of the atmosphere generated by the government.
Of course, the minister's actions regarding Exxon have nothing to do with any political consideration by the minister whatsoever, none whatsoever. It is just a coincidence that the minister is waking from his lethargy respecting oil problems in the country because there is an election around the corner. It has nothing to do with the electoral ambitions of the minister whatsoever. The fact he is setting Exxon up as the bogey respecting this entire matter and that this is merely a crass political move of huffery and puffery respecting Exxon obviously have nothing whatsoever to do with the election.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that they have everything to do with the elections. What he is attempting to do is set himself up as the Canadian white knight on a charger that is going full blast at that windmill called the multinational company, Exxon. Of course, this is not only ridiculous, it is almost patently dishonest, because if the minister was not aware that Imperial Oil bought its Venezuelan crude through its parent company long before the date he said he first learned of it in January, he should have known it. 1 suggest he did know it earlier than January, but again he has done nothing about it for years. Now he is leaning on the state-owned oil company in this country to get us out of the problem. I suggest that is no answer to the problem whatsoever, but again that it is a crass political move on the part of the minister. He is setting up his own straw men so he can knock them down, again with his own straw company, and that is no better an answer by any means.
The minister says it is a matter of government policy, his policy, that he is attempting to source most of the Canadian crude that, unfortunately, we need in this country in the western hemisphere. I suggest to him that a far better move by him, and better worth-while action by him, instead of attempting to shift the burden of Canadian needs from one offshore company and one offshore country like Iran into a state run company, and other foreign countries like Venezuela and Mexico, would be to spend half the effort, half the time and half of the taxpayers' money he is wasting on these other efforts in an attempt to make sure that Canadian energy needs are met by Canadian energy supplies. In that way we would be far better off.
The minister says, quite rightly, that we have been dependent for 60 per cent of our offshore crude on Middle East sources. Now, wonder of wonders, he is going to change all this and make us, instead of dependent on that source, dependent on Venezuelan and Mexican crude. To me that again is

another crutch, and we should not be leaning on that type of thing.
In this country of all countries we can, if we only had decent and meaningful national energy policies, produce our own oil supplies, our own gas supplies, our own hydro and our own nuclear supplies. We can do that ourselves. All we need is some faith in ourselves and a government that will produce the tax policies for that type of development, not only for producing these supplies, but as well for developing decent delivery systems across this country. In this way there should be no impending crisis in the Atlantic provinces next fall and winter, a crisis which the negligence of this government, and no other, will have brought about.
In respect of price the minister now says what a terrible thing it is for Canada, because with the Iranian revolution the new rulers of Iran, whom he misguidedly labels as Marxists, are going to try to charge the highest price the traffic can bear. Those are his words of just a few moments ago. He may be perfectly right, and I think he is right. I can see no way at all that there is not going to be at least another 15 per cent increase in international, world crude oil prices by September 1. What is his answer to that? His answer is: We are going to try to move things so we are not dependent on bad old Iran or on increasingly isolated Saudi Arabia. His answer is to again move to Venezuela and Mexico.
1 suggest that if Iran is going to charge the highest price the traffic can bear, it will not be very long before that trend is very readily apparent in Venezuelan and Mexican oil prices as well. Obviously that is the case. If the minister is that worried about the price and that worried about this huge hemorrhage of Canadian funds from this country to buy this amount of crude oil offshore, I suggest the way to stop that hemorrhage is to start turning some of that money inward in order to produce and develop our own Canadian resources and delivery system. In the long run that is the only answer, but how and when are we going to shock these people out of their complacency? Obviously the only way to do it is by an election.
The tragedy today as far as the Canadian oil and gas situation is concerned is not that the government is bringing forward a tired old bill that was first brought forward in 1974 for the consideration of this House, but rather that an emergency oil allocation bill is needed in this country at all. We should not need it. We obviously must have it simply because of the policies of the government which have resulted in our being behind the eight ball. We should not be debating this measure today. We should not have this bill before us today, except for a situation that is the direct making of the policies of this particular government.
As far as the bill itself is concerned, it has been described in the press and by others before the standing committee as a bad bill, an unreasonable bill, as an alarmist overreaction with sweeping powers. It has been said that the powers the minister will have under the bill are "absolute and dictatorical powers". These powers have been described by others, not by me, as frightening and unnecessary. It is said that the tone of the whole bill is one of "authoritarianism and federal centraliza-
March 13, 1979

tion". Others outside the committee have labelled the minister, if this bill is fully implemented, as a czar. It has been said that this bill is "a piece of tyranny", handled by amateurs with all of the professionals shoved aside.
I do not think any fair-minded and conscientious member of this House, no matter what political persuasion he may be, could help but agree that this bill, as far as its terms are concerned, is a bad bill. Certainly I agree with that criticism, and I could add a few of my own. The first criticism I would add, for instance, is that we are dealing with a bill that will be implemented at a time when the federal cabinet, and no one else, believes we are into a national emergency as far as energy supplies are concerned.
One of the major gross deficiencies of this bill is that there is nothing in the bill to indicate what a national emergency actually is. There are no guidelines, no restrictions and no limitations. There is no definition of what may or may not be a "national emergency". Only the federal cabinet on the recommendation of the federal minister will be able to understand and to know what a national emergency is, and only then and only that cabinet will be able to implement the bill. I think that is a gross deficiency in the bill.
Even the international treaty to which we are a signatory as a member of the International Energy Agency defines for international purposes what a major shortfall in energy or petroleum supplies may be. There is a 7 per cent figure there which is related to total consumption. There is no such definition, there is no such triggering mechanism, there is no such comprehension whatever in the bill of what a national emergency can or might be. As a matter of fact, there are even gross implications in the bill to the effect that it need not be a national emergency in scope, that a disordering of the petroleum, gas or energy market in only one region or area of the country may be enough to convince the government to proclaim by order in council that this bill comes into effect. Again, I think that this is merely a sweeping overreaction by the government to the problem.
I am not indicating that the government should not have this power. What I am saying is that it is an ill-thought out, ill-conceived piece of legislation. It is technically poorly drafted, otherwise we would not have amendments from the government before the House at this late stage of the proceedings. There is really no definition or triggering mechanism in this bill. There is no one in Canada today, including the minister, who can give us a definition of what a national emergency may be, yet we are being asked to give the minister sweeping powers in the event that he, and he alone, can make recommendations to his cabinet colleagues, whereupon the cabinet alone will then decide, in their ultimate and final wisdom, just what a national emergency should be.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us this afternoon an amendment put forward by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) on the emergency supply allocation bill which would widen the scope and activity of Petro-Canada in acting in the interests of Canada by allowing it to be represented on the executive committee of the International Energy Agency so that it may advise and be a watchdog for Canadian interests in the event
4106

March 13, 1979
Energy Supplies
of a world-wide disruption or shortage. We in the New Democratic Party will support that amendment.
The situation that we have before us in this bill is one that I think any witness of the committee proceedings or the debate would find of extreme interest in terms of the way in which the two major parties are acting in trying to cope with the ever-increasing energy problem facing Canadians.
As we all know, this bill will not solve the long-term problem of supply and security of supply for Canadians. What it does do, however, is give the government emergency powers to allocate oil in the event of serious disruption of supply. I do not see how any reasonable Canadian can be opposed to that concept, that of giving the national government the power to deal with what would be a national emergency. After listening to the oratory and the arguments of the Conservative party, I am still at a loss to understand what they would put forward to replace the bill which we have before us. They are very quick at criticizing and using generalities about wide powers and about the minister becoming a dictator, but in terms of any concrete alternative on how the minister is to deal with an emergency situation, they are not forthcoming. The Conservative party does not seem to have a comprehensive energy policy, other than to provide more subsidies for the multinationals that got us into this mess in the first place.
As the minister moved his amendment today, he pointed out that we may face continued shortages of oil from Iran, a shortfall of perhaps as much as three million barrels a day, half of what was normally produced by that country. He also said that we would be faced with higher prices. The minister avoided the very difficult question of where we would get our supplies if we were cut off either by Iran or Venezuela, or if they were reduced by any of the normal suppliers. I would like to address myself to that matter in a few moments, especially in light of the minister's meeting this morning with Mr. Armstrong, the president of Imperial Oil.
This amendment which we have before us, as I say, we support. In fact, it is the New Democratic Party that has been continually urging a greater role for Petro-Canada, our national petroleum company. As hon. members will recall, it was during the minority parliament of 1972 to 1974 that our party, holding the balance of power, was able to convince the then Liberal government to introduce legislation for Petro-Canada in order that it could act in the interests of Canadians.
