speechtext:
The hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Roy) has asked if I was in on the negotiations. I worked on the committee that dealt with the Petro-Canada legislation and was in close liaison with our energy critic at the time, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) and our party leader, who reported to us the state of ongoing

developments in the negotiations with the government to set up Petro-Canada.
Anyone who knows the events of that year will recall the demand which was made publicly for Petro-Canada, as well as a number of other demands by our party, and the government's acquiescing to those demands. As I have said, we are arguing for a greater role for Petro-Canada. Therefore, I can see only advantages in putting Petro-Canada on this executive committee of the International Energy Agency.
Indeed, I was happy that the amendment which I made in committee to this bill before us to put a representative of Petro-Canada on the emergency allocation board in Canada was accepted by the government, although the Conservative opposition voted against it. I have another amendment in motion No. 5 which argues for Petro-Canada, in the event of an emergency being declared, to become the sole importer of offshore oil. I will deal with that at the appropriate time.
When I looked at the statement made by the minister yesterday in the procedural debate on the amendment, I noticed that he too shares our view that Petro-Canada should have a central and important role in development energy policy. I do wish that what he says was translated into more concrete action. Quoting from page 4052 of Hansard the minister said:
-and it seems to me to be even more important now that Petro-Canada be included and designated as our watchdog with the other multinational corporations that will be involved in the implementation of that oil sharing arrangement. After all, all hon. members will remember it was not so very long ago when one of the international oil companies, Exxon, involved itself in the diversion of crude which was destined for Canada. It is in that kind of situation that I think it is important that Canada should be involved, in order to guard against this sort of thing.
That is a very interesting statement about the need for Petro-Canada, especially as a counterbalance to the power that the multinational oil companies have in Canada. We all know that our oil industry is about 90 per cent foreign owned, and that the multinationals have designed energy policies to benefit themselves rather than Canadian energy consumers. Of course, we are now literally paying the price for that kind of policy, and we are paying the price in terms of supply problems. It will be of interest to see what the minister actually envisions as a role for Petro-Canada in light of that larger problem, which is only partially alluded to in the amendment we have before us.
When the parent company of Imperial Oil, Exxon, announced that it would divert 100,000 barrels of Venezuelan oil destined for Canada, the minister announced that that was unacceptable, that no minister of energy or any Canadian government could accept an arbitrary decision by a multinational company to tell its Canadian subsidiary to divert oil contracted for eastern Canadian markets.
There was a great hubbub in this chamber at the time and the minister wrapped himself in the flag by saying that he was going to defend the interest of Canadians, especially eastern Canadians, who depend on that oil. He began to negotiate with
March 13, 1979

Imperial. That company announced that it had reconsidered and would not divert 100,000 barrels of oil but only 9,000 barrels of oil destined for Canada's eastern markets. But the minister did not stop there. He said that if Exxon or Imperial diverts one barrel of oil, that was still unacceptable to the Government of Canada. In an interview conducted by and reported in the Toronto Star for February 23, 1979, the minister is quoted as saying:
"If his (Armstrong's) Exxon colleagues choose to put Imperial in a disadvantageous position, then presumably they're prepared to accept the consequences".
Further on, the minister states:
-the situation will not be resolved to his satisfaction "until Mr. Armstrong has established direct contractural links with Venezuela".
In other words, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said, quite rightly, to Imperial and Exxon that it is unacceptable for a Canadian subsidary to take orders to divert oil destined for Canada. He said too that he did not want Imperial Oil to divert any oil, and he gave orders to Imperial Oil to refuse directives from its parent, Exxon. He told Imperial to begin negotiations with Exxon to relieve its obligations so that it would be able to negotiate directly with Venezuela for oil destined for Canada.
The minister stood up in this House a few moments ago and said that he had had a meeting with the president of Imperial Oil this morning who told him that his position had not changed, that Imperial would still divert oil destined for Canada and that it would not continue to pursue the course of direct negotiations with Venezuela for the oil.
In light of the minister's statement that any diversion would be unacceptable, and that if Imperial did not establish direct links with Venezuela, that would also be unacceptable, it now appears to me that Imperial has given a direct slap in the face to this minister, to the Government of Canada and to the consuming Canadian public. Surely any government which has the interests of Canadians at heart, any government that has any backbone at all, will not accept that kind of dictate from a foreign multinational about the operations of its Canadian subsidary when the operations of that subsidary go against the interests of Canadians. The minister was quite bold in the House and elsewhere. He said that if Imperial does not do what he says it will have to face the consequences. I hope the minister can enlighten us as to what consequences he foresees for Imperial Oil.
Will the minister take action, legislative or otherwise, to ensure that Canadian consumers in Atlantic Canada get 100 per cent of the oil that was bound and contracted for, or will he capitulate to this multinational oil company? Will the minister go begging and thereby embarrass all Canadians, and in so doing admit the problem that we have in Canada today, namely that because of the lack of an energy policy and of the lack of public involvement in the energy sector, Exxon has held the Canadian government to ransom? Unless the minister can announce otherwise, it appears to me that Exxon and Imperial have won and the Canadian consumer has lost.
The minister says that he wants Petro-Canada to enter into direct negotiations with Venezuela. I commend him for that.
Energy Supplies
But the crucial problem is, where will the 9,000 barrels of oil which Imperial says they will still divert to Exxon markets throughout the world come from? The minister has not answered that question, Mr. Speaker. Will we get all of that oil or not? If not, what action will this government take to protect Canadian consumers?
Surely it is obvious, with these high-handed, arbitrary and unfair actions of Imperial Oil, that it is time Canadians realize we cannot develop an energy policy in this country when we are held up to that kind of blackmail by multinational oil companies. The only way out is not the way of the minister of energy-to go begging cap in hand, or begging on his knees, to Imperial Oil and saying, "Please, will you give us that oil destined for us originally?" Is that any way for a minister of the Crown to be acting? Because it appears that is exactly what he is doing. He has acquiesced to Imperial's thumbing its nose at the Government of Canada and saying: "We are not going to enter into direct negotiations with our supplier, nor are we going to meet our full commitment of oil destined for eastern Canada". What a spineless government and minister we have if that is all that the minister can say in reaction to that arbitrary action by Imperial Oil.
I hope Petro-Canada can enter into direct negotiations with Venezuela or with Mexico, because we will get a much more secure supply of oil. But I do not know whether it can. I tend to doubt at the moment whether Petro-Canada can make up the shortfall caused by Imperial's arbitrary actions.
These recent incidents of the diversion of oil by Exxon and Imperial indicate how far this country and this government have been backed into a corner by relying on multinational oil companies for so long to develop our energy reserves. It should be obvious even to this minister that the way out of this impasse, the way to break the stranglehold of multinational oil companies on our economy, is to move more directly in terms of public ownership and public control over the industry.
We have a magnificent tool whereby we can do that, a Crown corporation, the energy company owned by Canadians, Petro-Canada. It	could	be	a	leader	in	terms	of	developingenergy policy. It	could	be	a	leader	in	terms	of	developingenergy policy. It	could	be	a	leader	in	terms	of	developingexploration, price	systems and, above	all for eastern Canadians, direct contractual links with oil supplies. We do not want again to get caught in the squeeze we now find where a multinational oil company with head office in New York says that it will determine in whose interests our policies will operate. That will not necessarily be in the interests of Canadians but in the interests of Exxon and the maximization of profits.
If it means diversion of oil from Canadian markets to somewhere else, Exxon will do it. How much longer can we in Canada tolerate that kind of situation? Surely any government worth its salt would understand that we have to move quickly and vigorously in the direction of a larger role for Petro-Canada. In the interim we must take legislative and regulatory

March 13, 1979
Energy Supplies
action to stop this kind of blackmail that Exxon and Imperial are perpetrating on the Canadian people.
If the minister does not take action-and there are options available to him in terms of a swapping policy and a compensation policy for Imperial-it is obvious that this government has capitulated to the wishes of the foreign multinational oil companies. If this government does not stand for the interests of the energy-consuming public in Canada, we will continue to be ripped off and be at the mercy of these foreign oil companies. The bill before us is important and necessary. The NDP supports the amendment before us.

subtopic: ENERGY SUPPLIES EMERGENCY ACT, 1979 MEASURES TO CONSERVE STOCKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very pleased today to hear the minister announce that he had asked Petro-Canada to negotiate with the government of Venezuela. It is a step that is badly needed, given the refusal of Exxon to continue contractual arrangements with regard to continuing the supply of oil to this country.
I am amazed at the response of the Tory party. They continually talk of getting rid of Petro-Canada. They believe there is some magic way that a group within Canada can be large enough to move in and do something substantial in this industry without the support of a national company. I am amazed to hear them say that we do not need this bill. They say there is no need for it because there is no energy emergency, that this is strictly an election ploy.
We had our first warning in 1973 which resulted in more than a quadrupling of the cost of oil and the worst recession in the industrial world since the thirties. It has resulted in such things as a $50 billion balance of trade deficit for the United States, it having to buy oil on the world market. This has had major efforts on the Canadian dollar.
We have now had our second warning. Iran has been one of our major suppliers, supplying 20 per cent of the oil for eastern Canada. The Iranians are now saying that they are only going to supply half the amount previously supplied and at much greater prices. Iranian workers in the oil fields are demanding that these supplies go elsewhere. The government of Iran has said it will not deal with multinational oil companies. As the minister indicated, there is great concern with regard to what could happen to other countries in the Middle East, such as Saudi Arabia.
The minister has covered the whole matter of the Exxon diversion. Suffice it to say it is important that our national oil company deal directly with the government of Venezuela so that we will not be forced into the situation where supplies that the government of Venezuela wants to send to Canada are diverted elsewhere.
There is another major reason for this discussion. According to a publication by the department, within the next 15 to 20 years we must reduce our dependence on oil. It must be reduced to 46 per cent of our energy supplies, then to 30 per cent by the end of the decade and to 25 per cent by the year 2025. Therefore, we will have a substantial reduction in the amount of oil available.
I am amazed by the attitude of the Tories that somehow or other the industry is basically Canadian-owned. The hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) made this statement at page 7202 of Hansard for July 2, 1975:
The truth is that Petro-Can is a socialistic dream. They have conjured up in their minds the impression that the petroleum industry is not owned by Canadians but is owned by foreign corporations. That is not in accordance with the facts. Canadians own the petroleum in this country.
I do not know where they get the idea that Canadians own this industry in this country. There is perhaps 20 or 25 per cent Canadian ownership, but as far as control is concerned it is not there. Foreign companies in the petroleum industry control 91 per cent of the assets and 95 per cent of the sales. To say that we do not need Petro-Canada because some Canadian outfit will come along and solve the problem is to say that those facts are wrong.
Let us look at those companies. Mobil Oil of Canada is 100 per cent controlled by Mobil Oil in the United States. Chevron of Canada is 100 per cent owned by Standard Oil of California; Imperial Oil is 70 per cent owned by Exxon; Shell of Canada is 79 per cent owned by Shell Investments; Gulf Canada is 65 per cent owned by Gulf Oil Corporation; Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas is 53 per cent owned by Continental Oil. Aquitaine is 75 per cent owned offshore and controlled by the French government. BP is 69 per cent owned by BP and controlled by the British government. These are facts. These are the major oil companies in the world and, as 1 have said, they control 91 per cent of the assets and 95 per cent of the sales in this country.
The Tory solution of setting up a group to control the other 9 per cent is just ridiculous. Sure, we need support. We need Canadian independence. But we also need a Canadian company large enough and with enough muscle to do some of the things that have to be done. I find it difficult to understand this reaction.
Those of us who were on the Standing Committee on Natural Resources and Public Works back in 1974-75 when we were setting up Petro-Canada will remember the problems we had to face. There were something like 14 meetings on clause 2. We are reminded of the obstruction by some of the Tory members at that time. There is a consistency here, at least I can say that for them.
There were three reasons why Petro-Canada was set up. One was to ensure a secure supply of oil for this country. This implies that it might not necessarily be profitable to do some of the things that have to be done. For instance, Petro-Canada has in the last year initiated drilling operations offshore on the east coast. These operations might not prove to be profitable. If this were a private company whose only aim was to make a profit, they probably would not be there. But they are there because we have a problem in the Atlantic provinces and they are there to serve the Atlantic provinces.
The second point in terms of supply is that if they do achieve a breakthrough and find a substantial quantity of oil, that oil

March 13, 1979

would not necessarily have to be exported. It would stay here for use by Canadians. That is one of the reasons Petro-Canada was set up. Another reason has to do with keeping an eye on the industry. There is no industry in this country or in the world, for that matter, which Canadians and other nations view with as much suspicion as they do the oil industry, and perhaps for good reason.
I believe the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark) before he became Leader of the Opposition supported the notion that one of the reasons for setting up Petro-Canada was to enable the Canadian people and the government to keep an eye on the oil industry. If the oil industry is not to be suspected, then one way of making sure is to lay the facts in front of the people. If the Canadian government keeps an eye on the industry and the facts are laid before the public and there is no hanky-panky, then everybody looks better.
The third point has to do with Canadian ownership. I have already spent time on this aspect, showing the degree to which ownership is in the hands of foreign companies. Then there is the degree of control. The degree of control is even more important than the extent of ownership. Lion, members may notice that with respect to Gulf, for instance, there is a 31 per cent Canadian ownership. Nevertheless, control is still in the hands of foreign multinationals and this is something we ought to be extremely disturbed about, particularly in a world in which oil supplies can be manipulated so easily.
There was no end to the disruption in the committee. As I have indicated, we had 14 meetings on clause 2 alone. The bill was being filibustered, of course. Finally, though, we managed to get it through. In order to do so the minister at the time, Mr. Macdonald, had to make a concession to the Tory party; the government was obliged to relax control over the day to day operations of Petro-Canada.
It is interesting to note that the Tory party made a big thing out of the fact that the government was failing to exercise day to day control over various Crown corporations; this was at a later date when issues arose about certain deals with Korea and so on. But a few months earlier they had objected strongly to the government exercising some control over the day to day operations of Petro-Canada. So that was given up in exchange for agreement by the Tory party not to filibuster the bill. I think we spent 42 hours in discussion of this legislation in the House and 25 hours in committee.
The Leader of the Opposition has indicated he would dismantle Petro-Canada. The hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) suggested only last week that the first thing his party would do, if elected to power would be to dismantle Petro-Canada. A couple of weeks ago in Saskatoon the policy committee of the Tory party indicated they would follow through and disband Petro-Canada. So I do not think there is any doubt at all that if the Tories become the government we shall be out of the oil business as a nation and the multinationals will be back in it.
The Tories have accused us of lacking a policy. They have a simple answer, which is just to move more oil to the Atlantic provinces as quickly as possible. They have made a further
Energy Supplies
suggestion that natural gas be moved to the Atlantic provinces. They have talked about supplying natural gas to Quebec and we have already seen applications from TransCanada for a line from Montreal to Quebec. The Leader of the Opposition seems to be talking about a supply line which would run from Quebec to the Atlantic provinces. The Tory government in Ontario has opposed this, saying it was ridiculous and that it would not make economic sense. They are also claiming that the Leader of the Opposition did not make that commitment.
The hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) indicated the other night that such a commitment was not made. I thought he did make the commitment and I believe the people in the Atlantic provinces thought he had done so, but at this point there seems to be no such commitment. At this point, though, TransCanada has an application before the National Energy Board for such a line and the minister has indicated that he would favour funding the line by moving exports through the line into Bangor, Maine, and so on. So we are moving in this direction generally, though the Tories seem to be stalled at some points.
As far as oil is concerned, we ought to look very seriously at the implications of Conservative arguments in favour of moving far more oil to the east. This would be most desirable, of course, if we had the oil to move. Already we have laid a pipeline from Sarnia to Montreal which delivers 200,000 barrels a day, and an application is before the National Energy Board to enlarge the line to take an additional 100,000 barrels a day. But where is the oil coming from?
As far as I can understand the situation there are 15 billion to 20 billion barrels of oil in the western reserves ultimately recoverable. Seven or eight billion of those have already been recovered. Now we are using about three quarters of a billion barrels a year and leaving, say, 10 billion still in the western reserves. We have perhaps 12, 13 or 14 more years of oil supplies left at the rate we are using it, that is all. We have not made any significant discoveries in the north or in the north islands. There have been offshore discoveries off the east coast. They have been discoveries of gas, not oil. If we expand this particular project, we may find ourselves running out much earlier than we had thought we would.
The other solution is to move more rapidly on the Syncrude project. The Tories are saying that we are not giving enough concessions and that the federal government should put up more tax concessions and more money. I would like to refer to an editorial printed in the Toronto Star on March 10, last Saturday, which indicates a very strong feeling, at least from the point of view of the Ontario taxpayer, that we are already putting too much money into this project and into oil projects generally. The editorial says, and I quote:
But does Clark not realize that existing federal tax concessions would provide almost 50 per cent of the capital needed by oil companies to build such plants?
This is a reference to the Syncrude plant. We are in this business in a big way, and Petro-Canada is our agent. This is one long-term solution we will have to employ, but the Tories

March 13, 1979
Energy Supplies
say that we should give oil companies more tax concessions, turn over more money and turn on the tap. That is ridiculous. We are talking about very expensive oil and about projects which are still running into many production difficulties. We are talking about long term financing, long term production problems and so forth. There is no simple solution.
I am left to conclude that there is only one rational approach to the long-term problem and to the short-term problem, and that is to use Petro-Canada in this emergency and in future dealings. We should be sending Petro-Can to negotiate with Mexico, which we have done. We should be sending Petro-Can to negotiate with Venezuela, which the minister has done. We should be getting a substantial supply of oil from those two countries-the minister has indicated 300,000 barrels a day-which we can depend on. We should not be at the mercy of some company which has movement all over the world and which can move its oil from one place to another as it pleases.
I think this major move we are making is an important one. It is amazing that the Tory party can get so upset about the dealings of Petro-Canada and that it can get so upset because the Canadian government and the Canadian people own a national oil company. To them there is absolutely nothing wrong with companies like BP and Aquitaine, both nationally owned oil companies, moving into this country and functioning at will. However, they do not want a Canadian national company to do so, and they do not want any concessions to be given to a Canadian national company. These are some of the things which disturb me, and they should disturb the Canadian public a great deal more than I think they do.
I support this amendment. I think we are moving in the right direction. While I do not want to see Petro-Canada taking over and running everything, I think we need a strong national Canadian oil company, and I think we should let it function in terms of Venezuela and Mexico.

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subtopic: ENERGY SUPPLIES EMERGENCY ACT, 1979 MEASURES TO CONSERVE STOCKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can certainly agree that the hon. member who just finished speaking is disturbed. One can easily see that.
Mr. Speaker, have you ever heard such a line of malarxey that all the government has by way of an energy policy is Petro-Can? Whenever they are in trouble, they wave the magic wand, and their fairy godmother, Petro-Can, solves all our energy problems. But has Petro-Can ever found one drop of oil in Canada or gas? The only gas Petro-Canada has found we have discovered is the minister speaking in this House. He has more gas than Petro-Canada has yet discovered. There has not been a non-private oil company or gas company in Canada that has yet discovered one ounce of oil or gas.
The government here is admitting in this legislation to a complete bankruptcy of policy. The first oil crisis came in
1973.	Six years later another emergency supplies allocation bill is coming in because the government has done nothing to solve our problem.

What is our problem? Statistics Canada shows that in 1976 oil supplied 52 per cent of our energy needs. In Atlantic Canada the figure was 87 per cent, in Quebec, 75 per cent.
The government has done nothing to change that in the last six years, knowing our vulnerability. The figures show that we import into eastern Canada now 530,000 barrels per day, so that 60 per cent of the Quebec and the Atlantic provinces demand is met by these expensive foreign supplies. That is the problem, and the government has done nothing to cure that or suggest any cure for it. Those imports are costing us $3.5 billion in 1979. They will cost our balance of payments $3.5 billion. The government has done nothing to solve that in the last six years.
In Quebec and the eastern provinces there is an oversupply for refining capacity. Most refineries operate at less than 75 per cent capacity. The capacity was originally built to supply the American market, now closed off, and the government has done nothing to overcome that. That will bring me to the oil refinery at Come-By-Chance in a few moments. This government has failed Come-By-Chance, failed Newfoundland, failed Canada, failed eastern Canada, and it has no policy at all except to say "Petro-Can".
Here is the government's story in verse:
Alastair, Alastair, where have you gone?
"I'm out to see Hopper-I'm now just his pawn".
Everything is Hopper. What is the good of having a minister and a Department of Energy, Mines and Resources when you ask him a question and it's Petro-Can? They have to refer to Petro-Can. Petro-Can has to negotiate with Venezuela. Petro-Can has to negotiate with Mexico. Do we not have a minister and a department and a National Energy Board so that we do not have to have Petro-Can do that? What a pitiful excuse for a policy!
Now, another verse: Listen to this, gentlemen. Please do not interrupt me when I quote my poetry.
"Petro-Can, Petro-Can," that's all they shout;
The Department of Energy has no more clout.
The 1973 crisis has lasted six years
With no government action until Iran brought new fears.
The answer, we're told, is to surrender all power
To the government that failed us in our energy-short hour.
That is all we are getting with this government. Give them more power? They have had lots of power in the last six years, and they have done nothing with it. Their solution is to come to this House and ask us to vote them more and more discretionary power.
Alastair, Alastair, where else did you be?
"Off to see my superiors in the NDP".
The minister is completely subservient to the NDP. "Pierre Trubent" and "Ed Broaddeau", they are the same. Tweedledum and Tweedle-dummer, that's the NDP and the government. They are in bed with each other. We saw that from 1972 to 1974. We see it now with energy policy. Where does the minister get his energy policy? From the NDP. Trubent and Broaddeau! The government wants to centralize all the power
March 13, 1979

in Canada here in Ottawa, and the NDP says, "Yes, we want that, and then we want to nationalize it too". That is the only difference between them, if there is any difference.
All the oil and gas in Canada today was produced by the private sector, and still is, except where Petro-Canada has horned in on a takeover. So this is the government which asks us to approve this bill. Well, I for one do not approve it, and I will come to another reason why I have no intention of voting for it unless the minister gets up off his duff and gets to work to help the oil refinery which has been closed in Come-By-Chance since 1976. In February, 1976 the oil refinery at Come-By-Chance went into bankruptcy. It failed, and this government has done nothing in the last three years to help it start again. Under the legislation now before this House the government is being given the power to make sure that that refinery never starts again.
If the government is no more successful in helping Canadians generally than it has been at helping Newfoundlanders get their refinery going again, get the 500 jobs back and get that $300 million asset producing, then we are in bad shape, slack shape indeed in this country. The leader of the NDP went to Newfoundland and suggested nationalizing the oil refinery at Come-By-Chance. Their answer is to nationalize it and to have Petro-Canada operate it.
I asked Petro-Canada in April of 1977 what they thought about the oil refinery at Come-By-Chance, because the minister had said he would ask Petro-Canada to look at it. You know what I was told by Mr. Hopper, the famous Mr. Hopper to whom the minister is surrendering? Now the minister is the complete puppet of Hoppers. "Alastair, Alastair, where have you gone? 'I'm out to see Hopper, I am now just his pawn'." Mr. Hopper said that the refinery at Come-By-Chance will not be needed to provide oil products on the east coast until at least the early 1980s. Those are dismal propects for the east coast since it went into receivership. They had consultants survey the plant, the report was confidential, but it certainly was not favourable. That is all that Petro-Canada did. I quote:
Any operator taking it over would have to be prepared to face some very tough years.
Petro-Canada is not going to take it over. How can it take it over? It is an export refinery; it is not needed for the domestic market in Canada. That is why it will not be taken over by Petro-Canada and the suggestion of the NDP is nonsensical. It is complete economic nonsense, as their suggestions usually are.
In the fall of 1976 the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) went to Come-By-Chance during the by-elections and told the oil workers there and their union that the refinery would be operating in 1977. But he has not done a thing since then. That was two and a half years ago.
On September 15, 1977, he told the Clarenville Packet, a newspaper that circulates in Come-By-Chance, that he had had meetings with three reputable companies to discuss the possible takeover of the Come-By-Chance refinery. That was
Energy Supplies
two years ago. Two of these were North American based companies with large retail distribution networks. Where are they? They have not materialized since. The article in that newspaper goes on to read:
He noted that a number of options are open to the federal government as to involvement by Come-by-Chance.
He said in talking with the United States last week, for instance, "there was talk of using Come-By-Chance and all other surplus refining capacity in eastern Canada on a basis that would help supply the eastern seaboard of the U.S. Canada would establish Come-By-Chance as an "in bond refinery American crude in, American finished products out, destined for the United States.
What happened to that? It was complete and utter bluff. There is another election coming now and they will not be getting away with bluffing down in Come-by-Chance while 1 am the incumbent member, and I will be the incumbent member after the next election, except that we will be in the government and we will be taking some action to help that refinery. That refinery produces 100,000 barrels a day. The bankruptcy amounted to something like $600 million, and the people who owned the first mortgage are the ECGD, the English Export Credit Guarantee Department, the equivalent in England of our EDC. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that our EDC will be following the course taken by ECGD before much longer. They hold the first mortgage and they are owed $162 million under their first mortgage. It is costing them $5 million a year to keep that refinery in mothballs so that it will not deteriorate and will be ready when somebody takes it over. That amounts to over $400,000 a month. It has cost them $15 million to keep it in mothballs and it is not operating.
They have scoured the world trying to find another party who would be interested in taking it over and operating it. The Golden Eagle made a bid but they are only interested in it as a transshipment point, not in operating a refinery. The only ones they have been able to find is the First Arabian Corporation of Luxembourg headed by a man called Mr. Roger Tamrez who is connected with a group of Saudi Arabians. He has sources of crude oil, he has marketing resources, and he has made a bid to the receivers under the first mortgage, to Peat, Marwick and Company Limited, which they have accepted.
A second proposal was made by John Shaheen who was the original operator of an oil refinery in Come-By-Chance. It was his companies, Provincial Refining Company Limited and Newfoundland Refining Company Limited, which went bankrupt. He was involved in this gigantic bankruptcy. He made a proposal to the receivers under the first mortgage, and his proposal was rejected because the receivers looked at it and said that Mr. Shaheen cannot raise the money he claims he can raise, that there is nothing to his proposal but fantasy. But they accepted the proposal of First Arabian.
So there is only one proposal in play at the moment, and that is from First Arabian Corporation of Luxembourg. They have already bought a bankrupt refinery in Puerto Rico, the Commonwealth Refining Company Limited, which went bankrupt in Puerto Rico in the last three or four years. So they have substance; they have already shown they can take over a bankrupt refinery. They have supplies of crude and they say they have markets in the United States. They say that if their

March 13, 1979
Energy Supplies
proposal is accepted, they can sell their product in the United States even though eastern Canadian refineries do not come under the U.S. entitlement program which this government is supposed to have asked the United States government to approve. This government has not pushed that, it has merely put it forward pro forma.
We have Point Tupper operating at 50 per cent capacity, a whole series of east coast refineries operating at only 75 per cent capacity, and yet this government has offered the United States nothing to bring us under the entitlement program so that these refineries can compete in the United States. They do not care about these refineries, they do not care about eastern Canada, they do not care about anything. All they care about is to stay in power and to hang on by their toenails, fingernails and their hangnails. But they will go out kicking and screaming because of their neglect of problems like this one.
The Newfoundland government is owed something like $50 million on the second mortgage. Local creditors are out of money. This week people from First Arabian who have to enter into a detailed written agreement with the receivers under the first mortgage were in Ottawa seeing various government agencies.
There are some things that this government will have to do if this proposal is to go forward. On April 15 there is supposed to be a final contract of sale. Local creditors have been told by Mr. Shaheen that he would see they are repaid although they are unsecured. I am referring to the local Newfoundland creditors under the original bankruptcy. That is all well and good. If the proposal of Mr. Shaheen was accepted and carried out, they might all be paid. But his proposal is not in play; it has been rejected by the first mortgagee who controls the situation, unless someone wants to pay the first mortgagee $162 million plus the $15 million they have spent.
There is only one proposal in play, and for that to go forward the Government of Canada has to take certain actions. One of those actions is this. When this legislation passes the House and the Senate, it means that the government can step in at any time they say there is an emergency and interfere with export contracts, with movements of crude oil, with the sale of refined products. They did that at Come-By-Chance in 1974 and 1975. Even if you get a term export licence from the National Energy Board to export your product, the government can interfere and order you not to export. No one, neither the First Arabian Corporation nor any other corporation that takes over the oil refinery at Come-By-Chance, can do so unless the government can guarantee that at least for a period of five to ten years they will not interfere with the sale of refined products outside Canada. Unless they can have that assurance, they cannot get the money to reopen the refinery, they cannot get the several hundreds of millions of dollars in financing which they will need. They need $50 million to repair the defective hydrogen plant and the other defective parts of the original oil refinery. They cannot get financing unless this government will guarantee them that there will be no interference in their export contracts of refined products from Come-By-Chance.

The refined products are not needed in Canada, there is no market for them here. The crude will not come from Canada, it will come from overseas. It is an export refinery and if they cannot get this guarantee from the minister and his government, their proposal cannot go forward, the Come-By-Chance refinery cannot operate and 500 people cannot work. I would like the minister to assure me that before the legislation is passed the government will give them that guarantee. I will not support this legislation if I happen to be here when it comes before the House unless the government gives that guarantee to First Arabian or to anyone else with a successful offer to reopen that refinery.
The second point the government has to deal with is the wharf at Come-By-Chance. It was built by the government and it is owned by the government. They are out by $20 million. The wharf is of no value to the government because the refinery is not operating. They have not had a payment on the wharf in three years. The wharf is needed now and it is for the government to lease that wharf to the successful proposer who will take over the refinery at a nominal rental fee for at least ten years so that their cash flow is assisted in the early years. The government should do that because the wharf is of no value unless the refinery at Come-By-Chance is operating.
May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have yet to hear the reason for attempting to change the name given to our country by the Fathers of Confederation in the year 1867. Some hon. members said in committee and in the House that the word "dominion" is divisive. If it is, in my opinion it is only so in the minds of politicians who would rather play politics than do something positive for Canada and Canadians. If any member of the House has received representations that the word "dominion" is dividing the country, I would ask that he or she explain or reveal the reasoning behind that type of thinking.
It seems to me more than strange that on the very day after the celebration of Commonwealth Day a private member's bill should be brought before the House which would tend to separate the nation from the Commonwealth of Nations, a group of 40 countries, as Mr. Speaker said, "of great diversity in terms of size, race, colour, creed and culture, and at all stages of economic development". Perhaps some members have overlooked the fact that the second Monday in March was designated Commonwealth Day at the suggestion of Canada in 1975. The Dominion of Canada is part of that Commonwealth.
According to the dictionary, a dominion is "a country under a particular government; self-governing member of the British Commonwealth of Nations". "Commonwealth" is shown as "the body politic", which is "the state or nation as an organized political entity or the people collectively". What is divisive about either word? I would say the very word "dominion" exemplifies one people: brothers and sisters in a nation whose ten provinces are members of that family.
Why switch to Canada Day from Dominion Day just because, in the words of some hon. members opposite, the former is the name generally used? I ask by whom and where are they? Sometimes even in the House four letter words have been used, but certainly the decision to be vulgar does not signify that type of language is going to be adopted. I would certainly hope not. What the country needs today are more citizens who stand up for the country, what it means, how it came about, the hard work and initiative applied by our
Holidays Act
pioneers. Canadians have not been given an opportunity to decide whether such a change should be made.
If the government is of the opinion that the name chosen for the country is not satisfactory, the government should bring in legislation in the usual way. Why try to sneak this change through parliament by a private member's bill? In addition, why tinker with this matter when the mandate of the government is running out? What is so urgent about it?
In 1976 when the bill was discussed in committee, a member of the government said the following in reference to the word "dominion":
It does have a divisive effect because some people do interpret the word as implying a link with another country.
Everyone in Canada has a link with another country. If we were to separate our words and thoughts from every country to which our provincial brothers and sisters are connected by birth or through their forefathers, would we have a Canada at all? Let us be realistic rather than petty. Let us work to keep this country the way it should be. We are all related as a provincial and national family. We can work together retaining our culture and heritage. We do not need more political manoeuvring, even to satisfy ideas in the minds of a few politicians.
I recall the fuss about Canada having a distinctive flag of her own. Everyone remembers the time spent on the selection of that flag. Whether we like it or not, and whether or not we admit it, the fact is the flag was changed because some people thought the Red Ensign was divisive. I did not think so then, and time has proven I was right.
Under a flag which is distinctly Canadian, what we have today is a nation on the point of division. A flag loved by the majority of Canadians who fought world wars under its proud and significant Union Jack and coat of arms of Canada was removed to appease a few, and I am not certain they were not all politicians. A new flag did not further unite the country. A new name will not keep the nation together either. The nation will be one nation without question when her people realize what they have in this country, when they decide to do something for Canada, when they work and pull together instead of imagining that everything of earlier years must go.
One could liken the continual chipping away at what we have and what Canada was built upon to a child who was given everything he or she wanted just to avoid discussion, argument or a bit of noise. Of course, hon. members know the result of that type of parental behaviour; the child is never satisfied, becomes discontended, and is seeking forever something else, anything to create dissension and enable the child to control the parents instead of the parents controlling the child. In other words, the tail wags the dog.
I am not an expert on the constitution, but I believe it is only right today to quote from an address by one of Canada's best known constitutional experts to whom every resident of the country owes gratitude, respect, admiration and loyalty. I should like to read excerpts from an address on June 19, 1956 by Dr. Eugene A. Forsey. They read as follows:

March 13, 1979
Holidays Act
Dominion Day celebrates one of the greatest feats of modern history: the making of a new nation, and a new kind of nation, by a handful of people of differing origins, differing languages, differing creeds, differing histories and differing interests, and in the face of obstacles that might well have daunted the boldest and most resolute statesmen. Everything was against them. The country was huge; most of it was empty; the Americans were pressing in upon the territories of the Hudson's Bay Company, threatening to cut off the new Dominion from any expansion west or north. There was hardly any industry: manufactured goods came overwhelmingly from Britain, and to central Canada for five months of the year through American ports, so that at any moment the Americans could strangle the economic life of Ontario and Quebec.
Central Canada and the maritimes knew little of each other, and many maritimers feared "upper Canadian" domination. Communications were poor: there was no railway from the maritimes to central Canada, and, what was worse, the main central Canadian railway, the Grand Trunk, came in from the United States and went out into the United States. If the Fathers of Confederation had followed their economic interests, there would have been no Confederation. They would not have gone to Charlottetown, and from Charlottetown to Quebec. They would have gone to Washington, and asked to be let into the American union ...
The Fathers originally wanted to call the new nation "the Kingdom of Canada". But the Americans raised such a storm that the British government took fright, and insisted on something else. The Fathers, for their part, insisted on something that would mark the new and higher status of the federation. Sir Leonard Tilley produced the solution, from the seventy-second Psalm: "He shall have dominion from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth". His colleagues agreed; the Queen consented; and "Dominion" the new nation became...
The title was a particularly happy one, for more reasons than one. First, and most obviously, it embodied the determination of the Fathers to bring into the Union all the British North American colonies from Newfoundland to British Columbia: ... as our coat of arms says. It declared the "Manifest destiny" of Canada to rule from the St. Lawrence to the North Pole.
Second, and more important, it emphasized the religious basis of the new nation. Who was to have "dominion"? The King of Israel, the Lord's Anointed: the King, under God.
Third, it proclaimed the basic fact of our two cultures. For "Dominion" is not Anglo-Saxon. It is an old French word which dropped out of use in French but was preserved in our English Bible and our English Book of Common Prayer.
Fourth, it proclaimed, no less unmistakably, our new status. The French translation of "Dominion" is "Puissance," (Power); "Souverainete" (Sovereignty); a far cry indeed from "province" or "colony", a foreshadowing of the independence to come. And it was so recognized at the time. It was meant, Lord Carnarvon told the Queen, just before the Act was passed, "to give greater dignity to the commencement of this great scheme." "Canada", said Edward Blake in 1876, "is not a colony or a province; she is a Dominion, under an Imperial charter which expressly recites that her Constitution is to be similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom".
Fifth, it asserted the "lordship," the primacy of the new nation over its parts. Canada was to be "one Dominion . .. divided into four provinces." The Fathers of Confederation had an immense respect for American federalism. But they had a horror of the "States' rights" doctrine which had nearly destroyed it in the Civil War, and they were determined to have nothing of that sort here. "The Americans," said Macdonald, "commenced at the wrong end" by giving the central Government specific powers and reserving everything else "to the States and to the people." "Here," he continued, "we have adopted a different system. We have not only given the General Government all the powers which are incident to sovereignty, but we have expressly declared that all subjects of general interest not distinctly and exclusively conferred upon the local Governments and Legislatures shall be conferred upon the General Government and Legislature. We thus make the Confederation one Government and one people, not five Governments and five peoples, one united province with the local Governments and Legislatures subordinate to the General Government and Legislature."
They made assurance doubly sure by giving the Dominion paramount power over immigration and agriculture, power to appoint Senators and Judges, power to appoint, instruct and remove Lieutenant-Governors, power to disallow provin-

cial Acts, power to protect the educational rights and privileges of Protestant and Roman Catholic minorities. They even provided for the transfer of the whole law of property and civil rights, except in Quebec, to the Dominion. Canadian federalism was our own, not an import from the United States; and we emphasized that fact by giving our central Government our own name for it, "Dominion," instead of importing the American term, "federal."
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to conclude this part with these words:
What is the fourth thing that makes Canada unique among American nations? Our membership in the Commonwealth, that world-wide free association of free nations which we have done so much to create, which Sir John A. Macdonald foresaw and sketched as long ago as 1865, whose corner-stone he laid on the first Dominion Day, and towards whose completion he worked with unexampled skill, patience and courage. This also is part of the meaning of Dominion Day. This also we ought to celebrate with full and thankful hearts.
Canada became a nation through hard work, initiative, co-operation, pride, and brotherly love, as well as respect for the efforts of our pioneers. Canada can remain a nation in which we continue to take pride if we all, as brothers and sisters in this family of provinces, and as a sister in a group of 40 countries, work together for the betterment of all Canadians, putting politics aside. Today it would seem to me politics and politicians are creating the feeling of discontent, not the residents of any one member of our family of provinces.
To change the name of this country would not alter the people's background, would not remove their culture or their heritage, any more than a person can change the colour of eyes or hair by changing the name he or she now has.
In closing, I want to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, the fact that there is a great deal of discussion taking place among the provincial and federal governments and among the Canadian people as a whole. It would seem to me this is not the proper time for us to discuss these small details that pertain to our over-all constitutional development.
I thank you for the opportunity of allowing me to bring these thoughts to the attention of this House at this time, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, in reading the very brief but very abrasive amendments called for in Bill C-232, entitled "a bill to amend the Holidays Act", I do not hesitate to say that I was appalled by the explanatory note that is included. The note refers to the word "dominion" in the Holidays Act as being divisive. This indicates to me that the hon. member presenting this bill, the hon. member for Vau-dreuil (Mr. Herbert), surely has never read the words of his fellow party member, some of which were quoted by the previous speaker, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers). I refer to the words of Senator Eugene Forsey on the term "Dominion Day".
May I just take a few more minutes to enlighten members of the House on his comments from an article written a number of years ago entitled "The Meaning of Dominion Day". I will just quote some of the excerpts which I think are particularly apropos in the discussion this afternoon. The first is as follows:
The Fathers originally wanted to call the new nation "the Kingdom of Canada." But the Americans raised such a storm that the British Government
March 13, 1979

took fright, and insisted on something else. The Fathers, for their part, insisted on something that would mark the new and higher status of the federation.
Sir Leonard Tilley, a great New Brunswicker, produced a solution from the Bible, the Book of Psalms, the 72nd Psalm, verse 8. I should like to quote from that, and perhaps we should read this more often in this House. It states in part:
He shall have dominion from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth.
There are other excellent quotations which I think would be very apropos in this particular debate this afternoon. The article continues by stating that Sir Leonard's colleagues agreed with him, the Queen gladly consented and "Dominion" became the new nation.
Senator Forsey continued in his article as follows:
The title was a particularly happy one, for more reasons than one. First, and most obviously, it embodied the determination of the Fathers to bring into the Union all the British North American colonies from Newfoundland to British Columbia: "a mari usque ad mare," as our coat-of-arms says. It declared the "manifest destiny" of Canada to rule from the St. Lawrence to the North Pole.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, it is from the Arctic to the 49th parallel and from the Pacific to the Atlantic. The article continues as follows:
Second, and more important, is emphasized the religious basis of the new nation. Who was to have "dominion"? The King of Israel, the Lord's Anointed: the King, under God.
Third, it proclaimed the basic fact of our two cultures. For "Dominion" is not Anglo-Saxon. It is an old French word which dropped out of use in French but was preserved in our English Bible and our English Book of Common Prayer.
Fourth, it proclaimed, no less unmistakably, our new status. The French translation of "Dominion" is "Puissance," (Power); "Souverainete", (Sovereignty); a far cry indeed from "province" or "colony," a foreshadowing of the independence to come.
Senator Forsey continues:
We celebrate, or we ought to celebrate on Dominion Day, four things-the continuity of our history; the duality of our cultures; parliamentary responsible government; and our membership in the Commonwealth.
The term "Dominion Day" denotes our history. It denotes our strength and it denotes our freedom. What word could more represent unity than "Dominion," from sea to sea? How can such a word be divisive? The Fathers of Confederation called our birthday Dominion Day. They called our country a dominion. It was christened that name. Surely to goodness 23 million or 25 million people in this country could not just go out and change their names. That is not the purpose. Dominion Day is history and it is the birth of our nation which we celebrate on July 1. It is the birth of our nation from sea to sea that we celebrate.
The term "dominion" came into being because of the birth of our nation. The name "Canada" was already in use before confederation in 1867. Therefore, it is definitely Dominion Day that we celebrate, not Canada Day. To proclaim July 1 Canada Day would be changing our history. I realize that the present government has the power to change our future, but I would hope that it is not powerful enough to change our past. Actions such as this can only be termed disgusting, distasteful and disrespectful to the Fathers of Confederation, who obvi-
Holidays Act
ously chose the name "dominion" realizing the duality of our cultures and the foundation on which Canada was based.
Last year the government spent approximately $3.5 million on Canada Day. This money was spent on something that will not even exist unless this bill is passed. I wonder if the government would like to see this bill pass simply to give them a reason for their very lenient spending and their madness with money.
Before this day last year I questioned the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) about the matter of funds being used for something which was not yet law. At that time I asked the Secretary of State if his department or any department of the federal government had proclaimed July 1 as Canada Day. July 1 is still Dominion Day. At that time I asked if the minister would inform the House whether the government, and in particular his department, intended to discontinue the law of this House and this nation in this connection and if it intended to introduce legislation to change Dominion Day to Canada Day. As hon. members may recall, the reply was minimal and useless, not to mention inadequate. In effect the minister stated that he believed that the Governor General may very well issue such a proclamation. He did not know on what date this would occur and he continued by saying that the government intended to celebrate Canada Day on Dominion Day again this year. It was a typical, irresponsible ministerial answer.
The government went ahead last year despite the law and misused their privileges in so far as the people of this country are concerned. How can any government ignore laws of this kind? How can the government ignore such heritage? How can the hon. member who introduced this bill ignore our history and past, of which all Canadians can and should be proud? The hon. member and the government ought to be reminded of the fact that ignorance may be bliss in the short term but to possess ignorance as one's attribute is certainly not a good thing.
The government has ignored the reality of past tradition. The hon. member presenting this bill is ignoring our past history. I quite agree that certain changes should be made in the government, hopefully very soon, and in the governing of any country, but we cannot change our valuable past. I do not see why the hon. member would wish to change our past history and to base it on what he alleges to be divisiveness. Our history is one of which we should be proud. I am sure that my ancestors are proud of the history of this nation and I hope that the hon. member is also.
What is implied by the name "Canada"? It does not imply the over-all country because that is implied only in the name "dominion". I would further remind the hon. member that the name Canada, although it is also a name of which we should be proud, was first employed in reference to provinces in the names of Upper Canada and Lower Canada, not the whole country. Therefore the term Canada Day does not apply to our over-all history.
I wonder whether the hon. member has taken the time and had the foresight to buy himself a chisel so that he might

March 13, 1979
Holidays Act
continue to change the name "dominion" where it is found on our beautiful Parliament Buildings? Does he intend to banish the gargoyles from the Peace Tower which symbolize our dominion from sea to sea and thereby give the literary meaning of "dominion" to the tower? Does the hon. member intend to restructure the arches over each entrance, especially the one over the east entrance which reads "Ye also shall have dominion from sea to sea"?
1 make these statements not only to ridicule the presentation of such a bill, but to ridicule its application. The bill is nonsense and ridiculous. In taking the name dominion out of our Holidays Act, the hon. member is creating divisiveness, he is changing our history which will certainly divide the country on the ground of historian versus historian. He is changing the terms used by our forefathers and removing the word dominion, which will certainly divide the country between those who respect it and those, if any, who do not.
The hon. member would also be changing the name of the day on which we celebrate our christening from a term taken from the 72nd Psalm to one which, although meaningful, has no religious background. Surely as a nation we should be proud to have in our history and tradition a name that has religious connotation. It will certainly cause the religious persons in our country, of which there are many, to be alarmed, but I guess the hon. member likes the word "division" or "divisive", because that is exactly what the bill is.
I would guess that the hon. member is simply following government policy in his beliefs. For the event of our last celebration of Canada Day, that expensive bandwagon effort, songs were composed. The English song was named, "Canada, I want to shake your hand", while the French song was called "Canada, a beautiful country-a free country." Would the hon. member like to see two kinds of Canadas, two meanings to the day which celebrates the birth of our nationhood, two celebrations, one in French and one in English? Surely not. But that would appear to be the reasoning because the word "dominion" cannot be deleted on the excuse that it is a divisive word. It is an English word and a French word, a word which means the same in both languages and pleases everyone. Why take away this word which means the same thing in both our official languages? Is it all part of a plot to divide this country?
There can be no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that the word dominion was used to imply dominion from sea to sea. There is no doubt that the word dominion denotes unity and, therefore, cannot be considered to mean divisiveness. I am reminded of an incident when I was on tour with some constituents from Moncton. We were looking at the tower and I explained to my constituents that the gargoyles were like arms stretching from sea to sea and that our dominion was signified in the height, the power and strength portrayed in the tower. A constituent asked if it would not be possible to make the arm facing Quebec a little longer. Of course, this could not be done because it would mean changing a structure which stands for all to see and as a symbol of our freedom and our heritage.

If the hon. member presenting this bill would like to change the name Dominion Day to Canada Day in order to please that group in Quebec which does not approve of our country or our heritage, then he would be changing our heritage just as if he were changing the gargoyles on the tower. It should not be done. It will create even more disharmony, and will make this country bend in the wrong direction. We cannot change history or tradition, nor should we wish to change something that we as Canadians should be proud of.
I close by reminding the House of what Senator Forsey said in his final words about the meaning of Dominion Day. He said:
The Fathers of Confederation laboured, and we have entered into their labours not just the fruits of their labours: their labours. What they built, we must work to keep and enlarge. We can do it, but only if, in the words of Arthur Meighen, we remain conscious of our mighty heritage, proud of the imperial fountain of our freedom and of the flag that floats above us, worthy of those ideals of British liberty and justice which have sent their light forth and their truth among the races of all men.
We must build upon the works of our forefathers, upon the works of the Fathers of Confederation. We must not change their ideals. We should be proud of our heritage and our ideals. We should not condemn and change them. We should not tear asunder what our forefathers have built well for us.

Mr. Speaker, like those who have preceded me on the floor this afternoon, I am proud of the term "dominion" for my country. It is derived from worthy origins. I am at a loss to understand how any member of this House could venture into using the terminology the hon. member did in explaining why he felt moved to bring this bill forward to eliminate the divisiveness caused by this word; anything but divisive is the word "dominion." [Translation]
I take the liberty of quoting from the Littre dictionary. I imagine that it is a derivative or another form of the word. "Dominion", which is the English equivalent, could lead to some misunderstanding or division. Perhaps it is the word "to dominate" which has led to that division but I see in Littre that the word comes from the Latin dominari, dominus, master. There is nothing objectionable about the word master. For example, they say in Quebec "master in our own house", meaning to dominate the country. But I read the meaning of the word. It is an intransitive verb which means: to rule supremely, to have supremacy over, to reign, or in wider sense, we can also read in Littre: to have influence, power, to surpass, to prevail. There is even a deprecatory meaning of the word, but I protest because there is no deprecatory meaning to the word "dominion."

Here again I turn to Littre where the word "dominion" appears as having been borrowed in 1872 from the Littre supplement.
March 13, 1979



1 quote: "The English word meaning domination, power, applied for the first time by the British Parliament to Canada in 1867."

I	see nothing objectionable about that. It is perfectly normal and perfectly respectable and something of which to be proud. Those who have preceded me have mentioned the origin of the word "dominion." They have traced it to the Psalms. It is worth citing not only the verse from the Psalms in English, but the same verse in French should be noted. I read from Psalm 72, the eighth verse. It reads:
He shall have dominion also from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth.
We find the French reads as follows:

II	dominera de la mer a la mer, du fleuve jusqu'aux bouts de la terre.

What is objectionable about that? That is Canada "from sea to sea." What this proposal ventures to do is to remove the word "dominion" from our motto "from sea to sea". These words are related in that one citation from the Psalms: "dominion .. . from sea to sea". We still have "A Mari Usque ad Mare" under our coats of arms. Why are hon. members trying to remove the word "dominion"?

speechtext:
I had something to do with the making of this history too, and I hope the hon. member did.
Now I will deal with this possible origin of the divisiveness characteristic of this word. I may have found it. The word "dominion" has nothing pejorative about it at all in the English language. In the shorter Oxford I read that it is derived from the Latin dominionem from dominium, which is a concept in Roman law meaning lordship, ownership, property. That is perfectly straightforward and that is perfectly applicable to a nation which is coming together to unite and have a power in its own right. There is a further definition which is the power or right of governing or controlling. Perhaps the mover of this particular motion would be prepared to negotiate that one fifth or maybe four fifths. Dominion means there is no negotiation. It means one nation.
Perhaps, where we run into trouble is in the variant to dominion to dominate or to domineer. They are semantic differences. The origins are somewhat different but we can sense them. There is something pejorative in dominating and domineering because those words relate to arbitrary rule, despotic or imperialistic rule. That is not what we intend by the word dominion. If anyone is trying to seek a means of eliminating the division in this country, I ask him to go back to the flag debate and read the thousands of pages of Hansard to see the division that that created. It took a long time. I know there are many who are not happy with the flag which is now ours, but they accept it because the flag under which Canadians fought and died has been removed.
Why was that done? Because it had a Union Jack on it. They did not stop to think that Hawaii, the fiftieth state of the United States, still has a Union Jack on its flag, as does South Africa. Maybe if we could get the council of churches out of there we would be all right and it would stay there. If I am not mistaken, Newfoundland has the Union Jack as its flag.
Why are we seeking to eliminate the divisiveness? I think someone is trying to create it rather than eliminate it. There has been a general campaign by this government. It has been obvious since 1 have been in this House that the government is trying to eliminate all royal symbols and emblems. Is that in order to eliminate divisiveness?
Let us remember that there are people in this country who may venerate these symbols and emblems. Why are you going to walk over them? Why not recognize that we in this House have certain attachments to traditions and heritage? Granted, this government not long ago fostered a heritage movement. It is not a department of heritage, but a heritage commission or something like that, which will preserve that from the past which is invaluable.
Terminology, tradition, and even the flag are parts of our heritage that should be preserved. I spoke of the Post Office. "Royal Mail" no longer exists. It is now "Canada Mail, Poste Canada." Let us look at the origin of the fleur-de-lis. It had its

March 13, 1979
Holidays Act
origin in the personal flag of Louis XIV. That is a royal emblem, so what are they kicking about?
The royal escutcheon and the Canadian escutcheon were eliminated for a time from RCMP vehicles. In the Post Office there is no longer royal mail.
I read the article that Senator Forsey wrote in 1956 wherein he reminded us that our first title was Kingdom of Canada. I think a kingdom without a personal king in residence is a difficult concept to get hold of, but not dominion. That is fine. Had we stuck with Kingdom of Canada, I bet that some of the anti-royalists around here would soon move to have that name eliminated.
As my friend, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers), mentioned toward the end of his speech, part of our tradition is the Commonwealth. I find it tragically ironic that the day after we celebrated Commonwealth Day as guests of the Commonwealth high commissioners we are here trying to eliminate the divisiveness caused by the word dominion which is part of the Commonwealth. I do not understand what the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) has going for him or what he thinks. I do not know where he found this divisiveness. Mr. Speaker, I would like to review for a few moments the history of the continuing campaign to destroy the heritage and symbols of this country of which we are so proud, Canada. This has occurred over the years I have been privileged to represent the people of Palliser in this chamber.
In 1970 Mr. James Brown, then the hon. member for Brant, the great grandson of George Brown, one of the Fathers of Confederation, introduced a similar bill. When it was sent to the justice and legal affairs committee, some interesting things happened. I was a member of the committee at that time. After hearing from Dr. Eugene Forsey, now Senator Forsey, a great and learned gentleman, the committee decided it would not accept the term Canada Day. It passed an amendment to the bill calling for a change in name from Dominion Day to Confederation Day. I am not here this afternoon to promote Confederation Day. I am here to promote the maintenance of Dominion Day, a proud and glorious name for the anniversary of the birthday of this great nation.
I wish to refer to an editorial in the Calgary Herald for Saturday, March 14, 1970, nine years tomorrow, headed "Desecration". I quote from the article:

Erosion of those historic traditions which gave Canada its distinctive character continues at a rapid pace.
It is now nine years later and the prediction of the Herald on that occasion has not been as they thought. The editorial continues:
Now there are people in Ottawa's governing circles who wish to expunge the term Dominion from living memory, even though it was conferred as title upon this nation more than a century ago and was made binding by usage and custom thereafter.
Mr. James Brown, a Liberal MP from Brant, Ontario, has a bill before the Commons' justice committee which would change the name of Canada's national birthday from Dominion Day to Canada Day. It would further distort history and pervert it to the use of nothing more than holiday convenience by having it fall on the first Monday in July, rather than on its legitimate date of July 1.
With this sort of thing going on during the past several years, it is small wonder that many older Canadians are wondering what is happening to their country and many younger Canadians are growing up not caring about it in the least.
Dr. Eugene Forsey, a political scientist, pointed out to the committee that the title Dominion is entrenched in the British North America Act, the nation's constitution. In other words, it is law. Not that this means very much to parliamentarians any more, considering acts that they pass which are of extremely doubtful constitutional validity.
The committee, making one of those empty gestures toward public opinion which have become commonplace of late, decided to postpone further consideration of the bill until after Easter. This would allow the public to comment upon the idea.
If participatory democracy follows its established course, no one will pay the slightest attention to what the Canadian people may think and another act of vandalism against the country's honorable heritage will be perpetrated.
Canadians used to sneer at the Russian Communists for rewriting history, making the past conform to present political expediency. Canadians need laugh no longer at others when they contemplate what is being done to their own past history. They can only weep.
Those words were written nine years ago tomorrow but, as far as I am concerned, the situation could not be more aptly expressed than it was in that editorial.
The effort by the government to change the name continued. In May of 1972 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) told us he hoped to have legislation passed in time for July 1 of that year. That came to naught. In 1975, another effort was made; fortunately, it too, failed. In 1977 the government again introduced legislation to change the name. The Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) stated in correspondence that he was trying to respond to the views of certain Canadians. He never told us who they were, though; there has never been an adequate explanation of the need for this change. I have to say I received many letters on that occasion in opposition to such a change, some of them from young children. I received a petition from six-year old, seven-year old, and eight-year old children attending the J. K. Malloy school in Calgary saying, "Please, Mr. Roberts, keep the name 'Dominion Day' because it means something to us."
What concerns me more than anything else is the fact that the government frequently violates the law of the land, for example, by allowing the CBC-I might even say encouraging it-to use the words "Canada Day" on every occasion upon which it refers to the birthday of this country on July 1. The
March 13, 1979

CBC should be using the term "Dominion Day", the legal name for that day.
It disturbs me to find the government constantly trying to subvert the law when it lacks the gumption to change that law.
1 hope that if this bill receives its just desserts it will go to the bottom of the order paper and remain there until the end of this parliament. I trust there will be no move to revive it by unanimous consent, no sneaky tactics for bringing it back again, and that we shall see the end of it. For nine years this measure has encountered concerted opposition. There is no real feeling in the House in favour of passing it. I hope this business will stop and that the government will respect the law and ask the CBC to use the proper term in the future for our nation's birthday.

It is interesting to note that since the OPEC embargo in 1973 which started the whole energy fiasco, Canada has been in an unique position compared to the other nations of the industrial western world. We have been the only nation which has had significant available supplies of oil and gas. Nations like the United States import large amounts of oil and gas. Nations like Germany, Japan, Switzerland, and The Netherlands, import virtually 100 per cent of their oil and gas. Yet every single one of the countries I have just mentioned has had an economic performance far outstripping Canada's. Every single one of those countries which imports its crude oil and natural gas has trade surpluses that are growing. Every single one of those countries has a currency that is stronger than Canada's.
When you look at the opportunities, the base strength that Canada has in its oil and gas, and when you look at the performance of our economy under the direction of that group of incompetents, and compare it with the performance of countries like Japan, Germany, Switzerland and The Netherlands, you have to reach the conclusion that something is wrong. We are not doing very well, given the opportunity we have of being self-sufficient. You have to be some kind of simpleton, a little soft in the head, to believe that Petro-Canada is going to change all that, that now we will suddenly start doing very well because we have a Crown corporation. As a matter of fact we have over 400 Crown corporations, growing like dandelions in April or May. If Crown corporations are the answer to our problems-I see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) smiling-how come that all our Crown corporations in the transportation sector cannot cure our problems there?
We have a Crown corporation in the airline business, a Crown corporation in the railway business, and a Crown corporation in shipping. We have about 50 Crown corporations in the transportation sector alone. With all those wonderful Crown corporations, headed by all the brilliant people whom the Government of Canada appoints to head these operations, people like Bryce Mackasey, we should not have any problems in transportation; everything should be cured. If Crown corporations are the answer, why do we have any problems? You have to be soft in the head to believe that Petro-Canada, a Crown corporation, is going to cure our energy problems. You

have to be soft in the head to think you can appoint former civil servants to be president and vice-president of this group and expect it will be a wonderful organization which will cure all our problems.
